hero.body:
A 25-year-old man died after he crashed his motorcycle while traveling at speeds over 100 mph in Vero Beach last week, police said. The Vero Beach Police Department posted on its Facebook page Wednesday that the wreck happened July 17 at the intersection of Eighth Avenue and 21st Street.

 Officers responded to the scene after a report of a deceased person in the grassy median. Police said the man was driving a 2008 Honda CBR1000 motorcycle, which left the roadway as it approached the intersection and crashed into a concrete utility pole.

 Investigators said the driver was captured on multiple traffic cameras along U.S. Highway 1 as he entered the Vero Beach city limits at about 12:30 a.m. on July 17. Video analysis determined that the motorcycle was traveling at 113 mph when it passed through the intersection of 15th Place and U.S. Highway 1, which is about a half mile from the crash scene.

 "Speed was the sole contributing factor as to the cause of this crash," police said in a statement. "This is a tragic reminder to please drive safely and adhere to the posted speed limits on the roadways." The name of the person who was killed has not been released.

cards.headline: Free and reduced-price meal applications open for Indian River County students
cards.teaser: Families in Indian River County can apply for free or reduced-price meals for students starting July 15 for the 2026-2027 school year.
cards.body:
Families in Indian River County can apply for free or reduced-price meals for students starting July 15. Students at six Indian River County schools can receive free meals during the 2026-2027 school year through federal nutrition programs. Other families in the district may still qualify for free or reduced-price meals based on household size and income criteria. Families are encouraged to complete one application per household to determine eligibility.

 To apply, families need their child's Student ID number, their child's full formal name as listed in FOCUS, a valid email address, and internet access or the LINQ Connect mobile app. Families who receive Florida Medicaid benefits need their 10-digit Medicaid case number that begins with the number 1. The case number can be found by logging into a MyACCESS account or looking at the Notice of Eligibility Review letter from the Florida Department of Children and Families.

 Families can visit www.LINQConnect.com to sign in or create an account, search for Indian River County Public Schools in Vero Beach, and add their student using the Student ID and formal name. To start the meal application, families should click School Services at the top menu and select Free and Reduced Meal Application. Families with questions can contact Shawn O'Keefe, the district's nutrition services director, at 772-564-5041 or shawn.okeefe@indianriverschools.org.

cards.headline: JetBlue cancels Vero Beach to JFK route in September, citing low demand
cards.teaser: JetBlue is ending its flight route between Vero Beach Regional Airport and New York's JFK Airport on Sept. 9, just nine months after the route launched in December.
cards.body:
JetBlue is canceling its flight route between Vero Beach Regional Airport and New York's JFK Airport, with the last flights operating on Sept. 9. The airline cited low demand as the reason for ending the route, which launched last December. Brandon Dambeck, interim airport director, said JetBlue was not seeing the ridership numbers it had hoped for on the JFK route. Dambeck said the decision reflects how the airline industry operates, with air carriers fluctuating based off of demand.

 Charlie Ahern, who regularly uses JetBlue flights at Vero Beach Regional Airport, said he believes the route would have grown over time if the airline had stayed with it. Ahern said the convenience of flying out of Vero Beach is hard to beat because it is easy and close. All affected customers will be notified directly by JetBlue and will receive full refunds.

 Dambeck said JetBlue will evaluate continuously, so just because the route is gone now does not mean it will never come back. The Boston route from Vero Beach is seeing great demand, Dambeck said.

cards.headline: Fellsmere animal sanctuary rebuilds with $100,000 after fire killed 11 cats

cards.body:
Ted Pankiewicz founded For the Love of Paws in Fellsmere in 2014 as a nonprofit in memory of his late wife, who had always wanted to start a rescue. The sanctuary serves vulnerable residents across the Treasure Coast by supplying 12 to 15,000 pounds of pet food each month to senior citizens, disabled residents and veterans struggling to feed their pets. Unlike traditional rescues, For the Love of Paws operates as a sanctuary where animals remain for the rest of their lives and receive care as family members.

 On March 9, a fire destroyed the sanctuary and killed 11 cats. Pankiewicz suffered burns on his arms as he stood in the ashes of what he had built. The devastating loss left the facility in ruins, but the community quickly mobilized to help. Residents rallied together and raised more than $100,000 to help Pankiewicz rebuild the sanctuary and continue his mission of caring for animals and supporting struggling pet owners.

 The new facility incorporates extensive safety upgrades to prevent another tragedy. The entire building is constructed of steel rather than conventional materials. A security system will be installed that immediately alerts the fire department when smoke is detected, eliminating delays in emergency response.

 An interior sprinkler system will also be added to the building. Pankiewicz acknowledged the sprinklers will likely upset the cats but noted the safety benefits outweigh the inconvenience.

 The rebuilt sanctuary will maintain its commitment to providing a home-like environment for the animals. The new facility is planned as a cage-free space where cats can move around freely. An outdoor catio will allow the cats to experience the outdoors safely while roaming without restrictions.

 Pankiewicz expressed deep emotion about the community's response to the fire. "The response from the community was just as emotional as the fire was, but in the opposite," Pankiewicz said. "The fire made us cry tears of sorrow, and the community made us cry tears of gratitude." The sanctuary will continue its dual mission of providing lifetime care for animals while helping vulnerable residents keep their own pets fed and healthy.

cards.headline: Waterspouts, lightning strikes and fires batter Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County
cards.teaser: Friday's severe weather left a trail of impacts across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County, including waterspouts in Sebastian, lightning strikes and brush fires in Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
Friday's severe weather left a trail of impacts across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County. Video sent to the WPTV newsroom from Sebastian showed a large waterspout passing over the Indian River Lagoon Friday afternoon. In Port St. Lucie, WPTV weather spotters captured video of heavy rain moving through the area.

 Merry Moore O'Rourke said her rain gauge caught over 3 inches. Moore O'Rourke described the sudden change in conditions, saying it got black, the wind started raging and the sky lit up like she had not seen.

 Severe weather stretched to Okeechobee County, where fire rescue crews airlifted a man to the hospital after he was struck by lightning. Port St. Lucie also saw significant lightning activity. Lucie County Fire District said crews contained a brush fire near the 1900 block of Castinet Lane after reports that a lightning strike ignited vegetation in a nearby lot.

 At the 900 block of Bellevue Avenue, fire crews responded to an evening house fire. Lucie County Fire District said it cannot confirm the cause, as the fire marshal's office still needs to investigate. Moore O'Rourke said the storms were radical and a little scary.

cards.body:
JetBlue is canceling its flight route between Vero Beach Regional Airport and New York's JFK Airport, with the last flights operating in September. The airline cited low demand as the reason for ending the route, which launched last December to excitement from Treasure Coast residents hoping for convenient travel options to the Northeast. Brandon Dambeck, interim airport director, said the decision reflects how the airline industry operates based on passenger numbers.

 "It's just the way that that market works, and air carriers will fluctuate based off of demand," Dambeck said. He added that JetBlue "just wasn't seeing what they were hoping for" with the New York route.

 Not everyone agrees the route had a fair shot at success. Charlie Ahern, who regularly uses JetBlue flights at Vero Beach Regional Airport, said he believes the route would have grown over time if given more opportunity. "I think if they hung in there, it would have worked.

 I think it would have built up pretty good," Ahern said. He noted the convenience of flying out of Vero Beach, saying, "It's easy. It's close." His comments reflect concerns from local travelers who appreciated having direct access to New York without driving to larger airports in South Florida or Orlando.

 The Boston route continues to perform well at Vero Beach Regional Airport, with Dambeck saying "Boston is seeing great demand." Grece Ezzi flew into Vero Beach on JetBlue from Boston on Friday for the first time, demonstrating continued interest in that northeastern connection. The contrast between the two routes highlights how different markets can perform differently even when serving similar geographic regions. While both Boston and New York are major northeastern cities, the Boston service has attracted enough passengers to remain viable while the JFK route struggled to build a sustainable customer base.

 Dambeck said the door is not closed on the JFK route returning in the future, noting "They'll evaluate continuously. So just because it's gone now doesn't mean that it never will come back." This leaves open the possibility that JetBlue could restore service to New York if conditions change or demand increases. Airlines regularly reassess their route networks based on seasonal patterns, economic conditions, and shifting travel preferences. For now, Vero Beach travelers seeking to reach New York will need to connect through other cities or use alternative airports.

cards.headline: JetBlue ending direct flights from Vero Beach to JFK Airport in September
cards.teaser: JetBlue is ending its direct flights between New York's JFK Airport and Vero Beach Regional Airport, citing low passenger demand for the route that launched in December.
cards.body:
JetBlue is ending its direct flights between New York's JFK Airport and Vero Beach Regional Airport, citing low passenger demand for the route that launched in December. The airline announced that service between the two airports will end Sept. 9, just nine months after the route began operating with much fanfare and optimistic passengers. JetBlue said in a statement that demand for this new route has not materialized as the airline had hoped. JetBlue will continue serving Vero Beach through its Boston route and has not announced whether it plans to add any replacement routes from Vero Beach or if it will adjust frequency on the remaining Boston service.

 All affected customers will be notified directly by JetBlue and will receive full refunds. Passengers with upcoming reservations on the discontinued route are encouraged to contact JetBlue directly or check their email for rebooking options and refund information. The JFK-Vero Beach route was seen as a major win for the Treasure Coast when it launched in December 2025, providing direct access to one of the nation's busiest airports and potentially boosting tourism to the area. The inaugural flight brought enthusiastic passengers who called the service a game changer for connecting family and friends between New York and the Treasure Coast.

 The route's cancellation comes as a disappointment to local officials and residents who had hoped the direct connection would strengthen ties between the two regions. The discontinuation of the JFK route after such a short period highlights the challenges smaller regional airports face in sustaining air service to major hubs. While JetBlue's Boston service will continue to provide some connectivity for Vero Beach travelers, the loss of direct access to JFK eliminates what many saw as a crucial link to the New York metropolitan area. The airline has not indicated whether it might reconsider the route in the future or explore other destinations from Vero Beach Regional Airport.

 The route had been viewed as important infrastructure for the region when it first began operations, with hopes that convenient access to JFK would help strengthen economic and personal connections between the Treasure Coast and the New York metropolitan area. The short lifespan of the route underscores the difficulties regional airports encounter when trying to establish and maintain service to major transportation hubs.
